entries.title: Mondelez sues candy brand Joyride over Sour Patch Kids dupe
entries.summary: <p>The West Loop-based maker of Sour Patch Kids said a rival candy brand is copying its popular kid-shaped gummy candy and signature packaging, according to a lawsuit filed Monday in the Northern District of Illinois.</p><p>Mondelēz Global, which also owns snack brands like Oreo and Ritz, described Texas-based Joyride as "a well-funded, private equity-backed candy company who wasn’t making friends on its own. So it stole SOUR PATCH KIDS’ popular look, and dared Mondelēz to do something about it." </p><p>In April 2025, Joyride released "Sour Smacks," brightly colored chewy candies in the shape of grinning people inside yellow-and-green packaging. </p><p>Mondelēz said in its complaint that the candy's design and package is a copy of its iconic kid-shaped gummies and yellow-and-green packaging. It also said Joyride announced a social media campaign in January 2025 to “usurp and surpass” Sour Patch Kids’ popularity by drawing more online followers. </p><p>Joyride Chief Creative Officer and co-owner Ryan Trahan posted on Instagram that he planned to make the company the most followed candy brand on the platform — a title the official Sour Patch Kids' Instagram acc</p><p>ount held, the suit said. Trahan, 28, is also a YouTube personality with more 24 million subscribers.</p><p>"Joyride’s strategy to associate itself with SOUR PATCH KIDS was successful: according to Joyride, its posts 'went viral,' supposedly gained Joyride 'over 300,000 followers,' and induced other major retail brands to comment on Joyride’s posts," according to the lawsuit.</p><p>Mondelēz and Joyride didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Founded in 2008 as Project 7, the company rebranded in 2022 to Joyride and hired Trahan. Its products are sold at retailers like Target and Walmart, as well as online. </p><p>Joyride's sour gummy candy and Sour Patch Kids are often sold at the same retailers and on the same shelf, the lawsuit said.</p><p>The company also disclosed in a May 2025 securities filing that it raised $30 million in private equity funding, valuing Joyride at about $100 million. </p><p>Mondelēz said Joyride was able to raise funds because the brand increasingly associated itself with Sour Patch Kids. The complaint cited Joyride's 2020 and 2022 sour candy packaging, which had different names, candy shape and packaging.</p><p>The food manufacturing giant is seeking permanent injunctive relief to stop the selling of Joyride’s "Sour Smacks" and monetary damages for financial losses.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Ellen Rosenfeld wins North Side District 4b Chicago School Board seat in uncontested race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/4b/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 4b</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Lincoln Park, North Center, Lake View, Logan Square</i></p><p>As the lone school board candidate in her North Side area, incumbent Ellen Rosenfeld easily won another term representing District 4b, according to Associated Press election results.</p><p>Though Rosenfeld, a former Chicago Public Schools teacher and district engagement specialist, had no opponents, she took in more than $100,000 in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>campaign contributions</u></a>, mostly from individuals — and more than several school board candidates in competitive races.</p><p>Rosenfeld first <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/chicago-school-board/2024/11/05/election-results-district-4-zaccor-rosenfeld-brown-day-gioiosa-davis" target="_blank" ><u>won her seat handily in 2024</u></a> against five other would-be school board members in the city’s most crowded race. That year, pro-school choice groups spent heavily to back her and oppose a teachers union-backed candidate.</p><p>She’s made serving on the board her full-time role the past two years after leaving her position with CPS Family and Community Engagement.</p><p>Rosenfeld is part of a bloc of seven elected members who have opposed the mayor’s appointees and elected allies on the board, who make up a majority. She has backing from the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents CPS support staff, and other groups that oppose the Chicago Teachers Union, the mayor’s former employer and key ally. As of last week, she’d received a notable $100,000 in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>campaign contributions</u></a>, mostly from individuals, though she was the only candidate on the ballot.</p><p>The former local school council chair and mother of four CPS graduates argues the current board has been too mired in politics and susceptible to outside pressure. But she feels the incoming fully elected board could preside over an academic resurgence, from a rise in reading proficiency to a decrease in chronic absenteeism, one of her key concerns. She said the next board must rally around a set of goals for improving the district.</p><p>“Without a shared vision, it’s almost impossible to get the good stuff done,” Rosenfeld said.</p><p>District 4b is home to 18 schools, including several high-performing neighborhood schools, coveted magnets and a popular selective-enrollment high school, Lane Tech College Prep. Families here choose their neighborhood schools at higher rates than in many other school board districts.</p><p>The school board district serves a significantly higher percentage of white students than the district as a whole. About 46% of students are white, 25% are Hispanic, 12% are Black and 9% are Asian American, according to <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=4b" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>. District 4b also has the highest share of schools that <a class="Link" href="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SVkXB/1/index.html" target="_blank" ><u>received the state’s top rating of “exemplary</u></a>” for academic performance last year.</p>

entries.title: Miami is No. 1 in first CFP rankings; Indiana is fourth with Notre Dame at No. 11
entries.summary: <p>It's been a confusing college football season so far. Nobody felt that more deeply than the College Football Playoff selection committee, which raised eyebrows galore in its first attempt of the season to make sense of it all.</p><p>Undefeated Miami received top billing in the committee's first crack at the CFP rankings Tuesday, followed by Georgia and undefeated Utah.</p><p>From there, the 13 people in that room could have been picking from a hat. Defending champion Indiana (8-1) was ranked fourth — eight spots ahead of Ohio State (6-2), which beat the Hoosiers 19-15 last month but has since lost quarterback Julian Sayin.</p><p>At No. 5 was Alabama (6-2) — eight spots ahead of Tennessee (6-2), even though the Tide is only a few weeks removed from a 16-point loss to the Vols. At No. 6 was Kentucky (7-1), followed by Texas (6-2).</p><p>UCLA, the nation's only other undefeated team, was ranked eighth.</p><p>Oh, and Notre Dame. The Irish (7-1) were ranked 11th — seven spots lower than their spot in the AP Top 25 — and that ranking brought with it a simple message: As the last team that would make the bracket if the playoffs started today, they need to beat Miami on Saturday or risk slipping due to a schedule that clearly did not impress the committee.</p><p>"A very, very good football team," committee chair Hunter Yurachek said of Notre Dame. "But when you look at Notre Dame's schedule and the wins they have versus the teams ahead of them, they don't have that signature win right now."</p><p>In fact, Notre Dame's biggest game so far resulted in its only loss — 28-24 at BYU two weeks ago.</p><p>Ohio State was ranked 12th, but would be on the outside looking in because Boise State, ranked 25th, would get the Group of Six automatic bid.</p><p>It would have been easy — maybe too easy — to blame the Buckeyes' fall on the fact that their offense is now in the hands of a freshman quarterback, Luke Fahey. But Yurachek said the committee was more concerned with Ohio State's defense in its 30-18 loss to a 20th-ranked USC team that hasn't impressed anyone so far.</p><p>Regarding the gap between the Hoosiers and Buckeyes — and the Crimson Tide and Volunteers — Yurachek brought up a blast from last year that confused most everyone: Head-to-head comparisons don't come into play unless the teams are in the same four-team "pod," i.e., 1-4, 5-8, 9-12.</p><p>"Yes, they had that loss to Tennessee," Yurachek said of the Tide. "But Tennessee doesn't have that same level of quality wins. Yes, they beat Alabama, but you have to go deeper" to find its next-best win.</p><p>Meanwhile, he said, the Tide got lots of love in the selection room for a win against Mississippi State in September before the Bulldogs disintegrated with the injury to QB Kamario Taylor. Mississippi State is currently 2-4.</p><p></p><h3>The rankings</h3><p>1. Miami 8-0</p><p>2. Georgia 7-1</p><p>3. Utah 8-0</p><p>4. Indiana 8-1</p><p>5. Alabama 6-2</p><p>6. Kentucky 7-1</p><p>7. Texas 6-2</p><p>8. UCLA 8-0</p><p>9. BYU 7-1</p><p>10. Mississippi 6-2</p><p>11. Notre Dame 7-1</p><p>12. Ohio State 6-2</p><p>13. Tennessee 6-2</p><p>14. LSU 6-2</p><p>15. Texas Tech 7-1</p><p>16. Wake Forest 7-1</p><p>17. Houston 6-2</p><p>18. Missouri 6-2</p><p>19. Iowa 6-2</p><p>20. Southern Cal 7-2</p><p>21. South Carolina 5-3</p><p>22. Arizona 6-2</p><p>23. Oregon 5-3</p><p>24. Florida 5-3</p><p>25. Boise State 7-1</p><p>The four highest-ranked teams determined by the selection committee will be seeded Nos. 1-4 and receive a first-round bye. Seeds 5-12 will play each other in the first round.</p>

entries.title: U.S. Army rep: Helicopters not hit by fireworks during Bears-Seahawks flyover (VIDEO)
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Videos of Black Hawk helicopters flying over Lumen Field on Monday before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ game against the Seahawks caused alarm because of what looked like a close call between the aircraft and stadium fireworks, but a representative from the U.S. Army said there was no issue during the flyover.</p><p>The four helicopters flew over the field during the national anthem, and fireworks shot out of the north end zone as they did.</p><p>Lt. Col. Cynthia Holuta from nearby Joint Base Louis-McChord <a class="Link" href="https://komonews.com/news/local/fireworks-appear-to-hit-military-helicopter-during-pregame-flyover-lumen-field-seattle-seahawks-game-blackhawk-chopper" target="_blank" >told KOMO</a>, the ABC affiliate in Seattle, “We can confirm that no fireworks struck the aircraft, no aircraft were damaged, and no members of the aircrew were injured," Holuta said.</p><p>Here’s a video of the scene:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">New video obtained by <a href="https://x.com/komonews?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@komonews</a> shows fireworks being set off from Lumen Field during pregame festivities last night - right as several military helicopters passed by. <br><br>JBLM tells us no helicopters were hit by the fireworks. <a href="https://t.co/GD5FaG8HCR">pic.twitter.com/GD5FaG8HCR</a></p>— Steve McCarron KOMO (@SteveTVNews) <a href="https://x.com/SteveTVNews/status/2117706489641210027?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>There was no indication in real-time of any danger or incident at Lumen Field, and the game proceeded on time. The Bears stormed to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/02/bears-big-plan-coming-together-beautifully-as-34-17-win-over-seahawks-pushes-them-to-best-start-since-2012" >a 34-17 win</a> over the defending champions for arguably their most impressive win of coach Ben Johnson’s tenure.</p>

entries.title: Incumbent Norma Rios Sierra, backed by CTU, holds huge lead in NW Side District 3a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/3a/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 3a</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Avondale, Irving Park, Logan Square, Belmont Cragin, Hermosa, Albany Park</i></p><p>Incumbent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/norma-rios-sierra/" target="_blank" ><u>Norma Rios Sierra</u></a> held a dominant lead late Tuesday in her bid to retain her school board seat representing the Northwest Side over lawyer and newcomer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/peter-gonzales/" target="_blank" ><u>Peter Gonzales</u></a>, according to Associated Press election results.</p><p>Rios Sierra claimed victory around 11 p.m., thanking voters “for the trust they’ve placed in me to represent the needs of our students and families," and sending “a clear ultimatum — our schools are not up for sale. Our schools are not up for closure. Our public schools belong to the people, not billionaires,” she said in a statement. Rios Sierra had 70% of the votes to Gonzales' 30% with 93% of precincts reporting. The AP had not yet declared a winner in the race.</p><p>“I can't wait to hit the ground running to continue to do the work that we've already been doing, and I think this just gives me the motivation to keep going," Rios Sierra said in an interview. “I can't wait to get to Springfield and really work on getting that funding for our schools.</p><p>“I think it was really scary to see how much money was being poured into this race, considering it's like a not paid, completely volunteer situation," she said. “It was really concerning to see how much money was coming in, and it was a little nerve wracking to think about what I was up against to be able to win this race.”</p><p>Rios Sierra was first appointed to the school board in 2024 by Mayor Brandon Johnson. She’s a longtime community organizer and one of four candidates who was endorsed by both the Chicago Teachers Union and the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, the formerly allied but recently feuding labor unions that represent workers at Chicago Public Schools.</p><p>Schools in District 3a are struggling with teacher shortages, arts program cuts, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/19/cps-revokes-aspiras-ability-to-operate-charter-schools-in-chicago-in-rare-move-board-of-education" target="_blank" ><u>charter school closings</u></a> and access to mental health support. The Northwest Side district has a mix of 23 dual-language, charter and alternative schools serving mostly Latino students.</p><p>While both candidates had similar positions on increasing funds for CPS and supporting immigrant families, their support differed.</p><p>Rios Sierra was one of only four candidates to be endorsed by both CTU and SEIU. SEIU’s political action committee and another PAC funded by the CTU <a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>contributed to Rios Sierra’s campaign</u></a>, too.</p><p>Gonzales had support from the Illinois Network of Charter Schools, a pro-school choice group, and the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and said it aimed to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.” Gonzales was also backed by the Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools.</p><p>Gonzales advocated for equitable teacher wages that he said could strengthen student test scores and expand opportunities for students, such as having a stronger trades pipelines and more school choice. Rios Sierra said she wanted to see more mental health resources for students and more art and extracurricular programs for neighborhood schools.</p><p><b><i>Contributing:</i></b><i> Ariel Parrella-Aureli, Block Club Chicago</i></p>

entries.title: Newcomer Brittany Kimble leads race to represent South Side’s District 6b on Chicago School Board
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/6b/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 6b</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Greater Grand Crossing, Grand Boulevard, Washington Park, Near South Side, the Loop, Douglas, Woodlawn, Englewood, Fuller Park, Hyde Park</i></p><p>Lawyer and Chicago Public Schools mom <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/brittany-b-kimble/" target="_blank" ><u>Brittany Kimble</u></a> holds a big lead in school board district 6b over longtime pastor <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/michael-l-neal/" target="_blank" ><u>Michael Neal</u></a> in a race between two newcomer candidates, according to Associated Press election results.</p><p>Kimble, who grew up in towns throughout Illinois and now sends her daughter to a CPS school, had 63% of the votes to Neal's 37% with 88% of precincts reporting. The AP had not yet declared a winner in the race.</p><p>Neither Kimble nor Neal was backed by the Chicago Teachers Union or the Service Employees International Union, the two largest unions representing school workers. Rather, Kimble came out on top in a battle of candidates backed by groups that are often at odds with the CTU and the mayor’s office.</p><p>Kimble’s campaign was endorsed by The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools. She received some contributions from the group but insisted The Urban Center has asked nothing of her. She also received a contribution from the political action committee affiliated with the Illinois Network of Charter Schools.</p><p>She said improving reading and math proficiency and fixing CPS’ budget were her top priorities if elected.</p><p>Neal was endorsed by Common Ground Collective, a new anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/16/michael-sacks-profile-chicago-billionaire-mayoral-race-brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-rahm-emanuel" target="_blank" ><u>billionaire Michael Sacks</u></a> and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.” Neal did not report <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>any campaign donations</u></a>.</p><p>District 6b includes 37 schools and has experienced some of the city’s biggest enrollment declines, while others closer to Downtown have enrolled more students in the last decade. A little over half of kids in the district attend CPS schools, according to <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by Chalkbeat Chicago</u></a>.</p><p>Black students are overrepresented (88%) compared to District 6b’s overall Black population (64%). Meanwhile, white families are underrepresented. Less than 1% of the student population is white in a school board district that is 20% white. Families’ concerns range from wanting quality, well-resourced public schools in all neighborhoods to feeling welcome on their children’s campuses, according to the candidates.</p><p><i>Contributing: Reema Amin, Chalkbeat Chicago</i></p>

entries.title: Alexi Giannoulias declares victory in secretary of state race as Democrats sweep statewide offices
entries.summary: <p>Election Day wrapped up with Illinois’ statewide races looking like where they have been for decades — with a full slate of Democrats taking the reins.</p><p>The state hasn’t seen a Republican as secretary of state in nearly 30 years, as attorney general in more than 20 years or as comptroller for at least a decade.</p><p>Tuesday night ensured at least four more years were tacked onto those counts.</p><p>Just over an hour after the polls closed, Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias took the stage at Mid-America Carpenters Hall in River North to a roaring crowd, declaring victory with a near 360,000-vote lead as about 26% of votes were counted and results continued to roll in for a number of statewide races.</p><p>By the time the race was called just before 11 p.m., he led by more than a million votes with 64% of ballots cast in his favor with 80% of precincts reporting.</p><p>But his victory comes with the complication that he’s also considered a front-runner for the fifth floor of City Hall. If he wins both races, it would allow fellow Tuesday night victor Gov. JB Pritzker to <a class="Link" href="https://lrb.ilga.gov/Commission/lrb/con5.htm" target="_blank" ><u>appoint a secretary of state for the better part of a full term</u></a>.</p><h3>Secretary of State</h3><p> Less than an hour before he declared his win, Giannoulias’ family arrived, his wife Jo Terlato beaming as results started rolling in, showing the incumbent’s early and large lead. </p><p>“Thanks, Illinois,” Giannoulias remarked simply, to yet another roar from the crowd. “Tonight, what I'm hearing is that there is a blue wave coming, and I'm so excited.” </p><p>Giannoulias has focused on maintaining “momentum on modernization” on the campaign trail, while touting the introduction of online appointments for secretary of state office visits and the installation of DMV kiosks.</p><p>He was propelled forward by millions of dollars in campaign funds, being left with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/07/15/alexi-giannoulias-brandon-johnson-potential-mayoral-candidates-campaign-fundraising-gap" target="_blank" ><u>$21.85 million in cash on hand</u></a> in the second quarter, with more pouring in as he announced his mayoral run. Republican candidate Diane Harris raised more than $6,000 in the same span, nearly the same amount Giannoulias spent to hold a single fundraiser in April.</p><p>Giannoulias’ rollback of testing requirements for older drivers became a point of contention on the campaign trail, as well as his views on automated license plate reader cameras.</p><p>He has said he wants to make his office’s audits of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/flock-license-plate-reader-explainer" target="_blank" ><u>license plate readers</u></a> more proactive, and that he wants to establish pathways for accountability after prior investigations found Illinois license plate reader data was accessed by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/27/flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-chicago-suburb" target="_blank" ><u>federal immigration agents</u></a>.</p><p>But no amount of money, nor his track record, allowed him to outrun the lingering question of his simultaneous run for mayor. Harris jabbed that the state deserved “someone who’s committed to serving this state’s office” in a Sun-Times candidate questionnaire response earlier this year.</p><p>When asked about his mayoral campaign, Giannoulias said he was “focused on today.”</p><p>“We're not finished with our modernization push, so people are going to continue to see changes that help eliminate the time tax, that focus on customer service, that focus on efficiencies,” Giannoulias told reporters after his speech. “So we're not done yet, and I'm excited about the future.”</p><h3>Attorney General</h3><p>Raoul also held an early lead against former two-term 2nd Ward Ald. Bob Fioretti that he never gave up. By the time the election was called, he led by more than 805,000 votes with 80% of precincts reporting.</p><p>The incumbent state attorney general won his last two elections by a more than 11-point margin.</p><p>Raoul, along with other states’ attorneys general, has successfully won the release of millions of dollars in federal dollars the Trump administration has tried to retract over sanctuary city policies, including funding for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/24/illinois-wins-suit-on-disaster-relief-funding-held-by-dhs-over-sanctuary-laws" target="_blank" ><u>disaster relief funding</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/11/04/judge-blocks-trump-administration-transportation-funds" target="_blank" ><u>transportation</u></a>.</p><p>Other lawsuits from Raoul's office have restored <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/06/appeals-court-kwame-raoul-trump-administration-medical-research" target="_blank" ><u>medical research funding</u></a> cut by the Trump administration and r<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/09/04/illinois-joins-lawsuit-against-second-trump-admin-push-to-cut-federal-funding-for-youth-gender-affirming-care" target="_blank" ><u>eversed a Trump administration attempt</u></a> to cut federal funding from medical institutions providing gender-affirming care to patients under 19.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Ebony DeBerry, incumbent supported by CTU, leads big in District 2a Far North Side Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/2a/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 2a</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: West Ridge, Rogers Park, North Park</i></p><p>Incumbent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/ebony-deberry/" target="_blank" ><u>Ebony DeBerry</u></a> has the inside track to retain her Far North Side seat on Chicago’s school board, holding a massive lead Tuesday night over attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hector-morales/" target="_blank" ><u>Hector Morales</u></a>, according to Associated Press election results.</p><p>DeBerry, a former Chicago Public Schools teacher with a background in community organizing, had 67% of the votes to Morales' 33% with 95% of precincts reporting.</p><p>She was one of the few candidates endorsed by both the Chicago Teachers Union and Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council amid the two unions’ feud. DeBerry raised more than $76,000 to stay on the board. DeBerry was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/chicago-school-board/2024/11/05/election-results-district-2-deberry-cullerton-hooper-doyle-leon" target="_blank" ><u>first elected to the school board in 2024</u></a>, when she beat out three other candidates.</p><p>DeBerry claimed victory and thanked her voters and those that supported her campaign in <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DfTm5ofEcnh/?img_index=2&dlrf=aW9ub3h2MDJjbW1y" target="_blank" >a statement on Instagram</a>. The AP hadn't yet declared a winner in the race.</p><p>“Over the next four years, I will continue to advocate for fully resourced schools, an expansion of Sustainable Community Schools, and increased mental health support for our students and staff,” DeBerry wrote.</p><p>She said education funding is an issue that “must be carried to City Hall, Springfield, and Washington.” DeBerry also reiterated her position of taxing the wealthy to fund CPS.</p><p>“The work does not end with this election,” she wrote. “We must continue our organizing for more equitable funding for education in this city, and ensure we do not fund our schools on the backs of our working class.”</p><p>District 2a is home to a large number of immigrant families. More than 80 languages are spoken throughout the Rogers Park neighborhood alone, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://rpba.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/RPB_OpenForBiz_FA-2017.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Rogers Park Business Alliance</u></a>.</p><p>The district’s 18 schools serve a diverse group of students, too. Around 33% are Hispanic, nearly 26% are Asian American, 22% are Black and almost 15% are white, according to <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=2a" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>. CPS students in this district are more likely to choose their neighborhood schools compared to the city overall. More than 40% of high school students attend their neighborhood schools, compared with only 24% across the city.</p><p>The two candidates’ views differed on how to fund and invest in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/10/16/six-schools-spanish-programs-cps-seeks-to-eliminate-language-deserts-dual-language-world-language" target="_blank" ><u>bilingual and dual-language education programs</u></a> while also addressing CPS’ budget deficit.</p><p>“We have to find ways to make corporations, millionaires, and billionaires pay their fair share,” DeBerry said in an interview leading up to the election, while Morales said board members “need to make sure we’re using what we got now, before we start asking folks for more money.”</p><p>DeBerry <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/chicago-school-board/2024/11/05/election-results-district-2-deberry-cullerton-hooper-doyle-leon" target="_blank" ><u>won 43% of the vote in 2024</u></a>, edging out three other candidates.</p><p>DeBerry was one of four candidates who was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/09/21/key-education-endorsements-for-cps-school-board-candidates" target="_blank" ><u>endorsed by both the </u></a>CTU and SEIU, which represents CPS support staff. Political action committees for both unions <a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>contributed to DeBerry’s campaign</u></a>, too.</p><p>Morales was endorsed by the <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DcLn64Ikau1/?img_index=3" target="_blank" ><u>Common Ground Collective</u></a>, a political action committee that is anti-CTU, heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and said it aimed to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”</p><p>Morales was also endorsed by The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools.</p><p><i>Contributing: Molly DeVore, Block Club Chicago</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago Teachers Union poised to capture half of school board district seats but likely to lose presidency
entries.summary: <p>Despite being massively outspent, the Chicago Teachers Union was leading in nine of the 20 school board seats as of 9 p.m. Tuesday, according to election results from the Associated Press. That would be enough to throw up formidable opposition to classroom cuts, school closures and other measures that they see as contrary to its progressive agenda.</p><p>A 10th candidate backed by the CTU-funded political group Our Schools also appeared to have won.</p><p>The CTU’s candidate for board president, Hilario Dominguez, was trailing Jessica Biggs at that time. But if the teachers union secures a nine-member bloc, it would be enough to give a non-CTU-backed president like Biggs trouble.</p><p>CTU’s biggest opponent in this race was billionaire and former Mayor Rahm Emanuel adviser Michael Sacks and the political group Common Ground Collective, into which Sacks put $6.8 million over the past two months. Common Ground Collective appeared to have only won three contested races, though the group endorsed an additional five unopposed candidates.</p><p>Biggs took money from Sacks but was not formally endorsed by the Common Ground Collective. If the CTU secures those nine seats and Biggs wins the president’s seat, she would lack the two-thirds majority needed to overturn any resolutions that may pass at December’s board meeting, where sitting board members will cast votes for the final time.</p><p>The current school board, half of which is appointed by Mayor Brandon Johnson and is aligned with the CTU, could approve a moratorium on school closings and try to tie the incoming board’s hands when it comes to future cuts.</p><p>The CTU did not have candidates in five of the 20 district races after failing to put up candidates in two of those races, while three of their candidates got pushed off the ballot through petition challenges.</p><p>CTU-backed candidates were leading in nine of the 15 contested district races as of 9 p.m Tuesday. Yesenia Lopez, who got the CTU’s backing in 2024 and was endorsed by the CTU-funded political group Our Schools this time around, was also in the lead. While she doesn’t vote in lockstep with CTU-backed candidates, she often votes in line with them.</p><p>The CTU was outspent by a 4-1 margin with investment banker Sacks alone pumping more than $8 million into the races.</p><p>Biggs, a current school board member and former principal, billed herself as a consensus-builder and, on the campaign trail, often pointed to her “broad coalition” of support, including the Service Employees International Union, which represents support staff in CPS.</p><p>If Biggs wins and the CTU secures those nine seats, the CTU-backed members would likely assume their position on the board with animosity toward Biggs. She took $1 million from Sacks and Common Ground Collective, the Sacks-backed political group that funneled $2.6 million into efforts opposing Dominguez, the CTU’s candidate.</p><p>Common Ground Collective ran commercials against Dominguez that contained half-truths about a misconduct allegation and continued repeating them even after the CPS inspector general <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/16/insufficient-evidence-that-chicago-school-board-candidate-engaged-in-sexual-misconduct-watchdog-report-finds" target="_blank" ><u>found the allegations to be unsubstantiated</u></a>.</p><p>Biggs did not speak out against those ads and benefited from them — a fact CTU officials and board members will likely remember as they think about working with Biggs and her allies. Dominguez, who was on leave from his job as CTU deputy political director, will likely return to his post if he loses.</p><p>Many experts say that Sacks was so involved because he saw the school board race as a proxy for the mayor’s race in February. Sacks and the business community have already contributed a lot of money to Alexi Giannoulias, who they are hoping can defeat Johnson.</p><p>A strong showing by the teachers union could be a good omen for Johnson, but in general, teacher unions tend to do well in school board races, said Jeffrey R. Henig, a professor emeritus at Columbia University’s Teachers College, who co-wrote a book about outside money in school board elections.</p><p>Voters trust teachers to know what should be happening in schools, and they also dislike outsiders trying to impose their will, he said.</p><p>“In school board races and in other state and local races, candidates have been able to defeat folks who have bigger campaign budgets by pointing a finger and saying, ‘This person is being funded by billionaires who have no investment in public education,’” Henig said.</p><h3>CTU’s backing in school board appears not as toxic as some thought</h3><p>Retired teacher and incumbent Karen Zaccor said that when she knocked on doors in District 4a, which includes Uptown and some of Lake View on the North Side, few voters asked her about her CTU endorsement or said they were against the CTU. In fact, many people she came across were teachers or had teachers in their family, she said.</p><p>“More people were anxious about the wealthy swaying the election and taking away seats from more qualified candidates,” she said.</p><p>Zaccor only got $34,000 from the Our Schools political group, while a trio of anti-CTU groups — the Common Ground Collective, the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and The Urban Center — spent more than $700,000 either supporting her opponent or opposing Zaccor.</p><p>Zaccor was leading as of 9 p.m., as was Debby Pope, another incumbent, former teacher and CTU stalwart who represents District 2b, just to the north of Zaccor’s area.</p><p>Some CTU-aligned newcomers were leading too. Connie Anderson, a mom who ran to represent District 10b, which stretches across the Far Southeast Side of the city, was ahead as of 9 p.m. Tuesday.</p><p>Anderson said she came across a lot of working-class families who liked her message of fighting for more equitable schools and making sure that the board was student-centered.</p><p>“We received really good reviews,” she said.</p><p>She was ahead of Patrick Watson, a legislative aide for 9th Ward Ald. Anthony Beale, one of Johnson’s harshest critics on City Council, despite raising significantly less. Watson got about $500,000 from anti-CTU political groups — four times more than Anderson got from Our Schools.</p><h3>District’s budget will be top of agenda for new board</h3><p>The newly elected school board members will be seated on Jan. 15, 2027. But what happens over the next two months will have big consequences for the start of their term.</p><p>In July, CTU-backed school board members voted for a budget that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" target="_blank" ><u>counts on $150 million in uncommitted revenue from the state</u></a>. They did this to bring back some of the 1,000-plus teachers and other staff who were <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/15/cps-will-cut-teachers-and-five-student-non-attendance-days-as-district-looks-to-close-budget-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>laid off earlier in the summer</u></a> to close CPS’ $732 million deficit.</p><p>The state legislature, however, has not approved any additional money and will not be back in Springfield until next week’s veto session. CTU President Stacy Davis Gates said regardless of who won the election, she and others will be in Springfield to fight for that money.</p><p>Yet if it doesn’t come through, the new school board will likely have to figure out how to curtail expenses to balance CPS’ budget. It is unclear exactly how out of whack the district’s budget would be without additional state funding.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/10/01/teachers-and-school-leaders-navigate-uncertainty-as-layoffs-are-reversed/" target="_blank" ><u>Chalkbeat Chicago reported in early October</u></a> that CPS had hired back only 350 teachers. If that holds true, it would mean an additional $35 million cost — much less than the $150 million added by the board.</p><p>Still, if there is a significant hole, the new board will have to figure out how to close it. That could mean turning to staff furloughs or midyear layoffs.</p><p>Hal Woods, chief of policy at the advocacy organization Kids First, said he does not think some board members understand how limited their options are.</p><p>“Are you going to cut teachers? Are you going to cut aides?” he said. “When you have teachers and parents coming to the board meeting saying, ‘You are cutting my school,’ that puts school board members in a tough position.”</p>

entries.title: Alex Giannoulias se declara ganador mientras los demócratas se mantienen en cargos estatales
entries.summary: <p>El día de las elecciones concluyó con las contiendas estatales de Illinois pareciendo destinadas a quedar donde han estado durante décadas: con una lista completa de demócratas asumiendo el mando.</p><p>El estado no ha tenido un republicano como secretario de Estado en casi 30 años, como fiscal general en más de 20 años ni como contralor por al menos una década.</p><p>La noche del martes pareció asegurar al menos cuatro años más para cada uno de esos cargos.</p><p>A poco más de una hora del cierre de los centros de votación, el secretario de Estado Alexi Giannoulias subió al escenario en Mid-America Carpenters Hall, en River North, ante una multitud entusiasta, declarando la victoria con una ventaja de casi 360,000 votos cuando se había contado alrededor del 26% de los votos y los resultados seguían llegando en varias contiendas estatales.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-690000" name="module-690000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Para las 9:30 p.m., encabezaba la contienda por más de 72,000 votos con alrededor del 56% contado.</p><p>Pero la declaración de victoria de Giannoulias trae la complicación de que también es considerado favorito para la quinta planta del Ayuntamiento. Si gana ambas contiendas, permitiría que el gobernador y también ganador del martes por la noche, JB Pritzker, <a class="Link" href="https://lrb.ilga.gov/Commission/lrb/con5.htm" target="_blank" >nombre a un secretario de Estado por buena parte de un mandato completo</a>.</p><h3>Secretario de Estado</h3><p>Menos de una hora antes, llegó la familia de Giannoulias; su esposa radiante, Jo Terlato, mientras empezaban a llegar los primeros resultados que mostraban la amplia ventaja inicial del titular.</p><p>“Gracias, Illinois”, dijo Giannoulias, recibiendo otra ovación del público.</p><p>Giannoulias se centró en mantener “el impulso en la modernización” durante la campaña, al tiempo que promovía la introducción de citas en línea para las visitas a la oficina del secretario de Estado y la instalación de quioscos del Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV).</p><p>Avanzó impulsado por millones de dólares en fondos de campaña, quedando con <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/07/15/alexi-giannoulias-brandon-johnson-potential-mayoral-candidates-campaign-fundraising-gap" target="_blank" >$21.85 millones en efectivo</a> al cierre del segundo trimestre, y entraron más fondos cuando anunció su candidatura a la alcaldía. La candidata republicana Diane Harris recaudó poco más de $6,000 en ese mismo periodo, casi la misma cantidad que Giannoulias gastó en un único evento de recaudación en abril.</p><p>La eliminación de los requisitos de examen para conductores de mayor edad por parte de Giannoulias se convirtió en un punto de discordia en la campaña, al igual que sus posturas sobre las cámaras lectoras automatizadas de matrículas.</p><p>Ha dicho que quiere que las auditorías de su oficina sobre los lectores de placas sean más proactivas, y que desea establecer vías de responsabilidad después de que investigaciones previas encontraran que datos de lectores de matrículas de Illinois fueron accedidos por agentes federales de inmigración.</p><p>Pero ni el dinero ni su historial le permitieron escapar de la pregunta persistente sobre su candidatura simultánea a la alcaldía. Harris atacó que el estado merecía “a alguien que esté comprometido a servir en el cargo estatal” en una respuesta al cuestionario de candidatos del Sun-Times a principios de este año.</p><p>Cuando le preguntaron por su campaña municipal, dijo que estaba “enfocado en el hoy”.</p><p>“Todavía no hemos terminado con nuestro empuje de modernización, así que la gente seguirá viendo cambios que ayuden a eliminar el impuesto del tiempo, que se centren en el servicio al cliente y en la eficiencia”, dijo Giannoulias a los periodistas tras su discurso. “Así que no hemos terminado, y estoy entusiasmado con el futuro.”</p><h3>Fiscal General</h3><p>Raoul también tuvo una ventaja temprana de más de 595,000 votos frente al ex concejal de dos mandatos del 2.º distrito, Bob Fioretti, con el 57% de los votos contados.</p><p>El fiscal general titular del estado desde 2019 había ganado sus dos últimas elecciones por más de 11 puntos porcentuales.</p><p>Raoul, junto con otros fiscales generales estatales, logró que se liberaran millones de dólares federales que la administración de Trump intentó retirar por las políticas de ciudades santuario, incluyendo fondos para ayuda por desastres y para transporte.</p><p>Otras demandas de su oficina han recuperado fondos para investigación médica recortados por la administración de Trump y han revertido un intento de esa administración de cortar fondos federales a instituciones médicas que brindan atención afirmativa de género a pacientes menores de 19 años.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.summary: <p>When Chicagoans are making history Tuesday as they elect all 21 members of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" ><u>city’s school board</u></a> for the first time.</p><p>The showdown for the school board was the marquee race on the ballot, with Gov. JB Pritzker easily winning a third term and Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton securing retiring U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin’s seat.</p><p>Many are closely watching the citywide race for school board president — a powerful position that sets the board’s agenda and, until now, has never been elected. Sitting school board member <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/jessica-biggs/" target="_blank" ><u>Jessica Biggs</u></a> has declared victory in that race, though the Associated Press had yet to call that contest as of 10:30 p.m.</p><p>Political action committees and individuals <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>funneled more than $5 million</u></a> into that heated three-way race, which also included former deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>Hilario Dominguez</u></a> and prominent defense attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Victor Henderson</u></a>.</p><p>How the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/11/03/chicago-teachers-union-poised-to-capture-half-of-school-board-district-seats-but-likely-to-lose-presidency" >balance of power shakes out</a> on the school board could be a harbinger of February’s mayoral race. entries.title: Incumbent Ed Bannon concedes to Margie Luczak in Far Northwest Side District 1a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/esb/school-board/districts/1a/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 1a</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: O’Hare, Norwood Park, Forest Glen, Jefferson Park, Dunning, Edison Park</i></p><p>Retired police officer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/margie-b-luczak/" target="_blank" ><u>Margie Luczak</u></a> unseated incumbent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/ed-bannon/" target="_blank" ><u>Ed Bannon</u></a> Tuesday night to become the Far Northwest Side’s new representative on the now fully elected school board.</p><p>Luczak prevailed thanks to big spending by anti-Chicago Teachers Union groups that put three times as much money behind her as her opponent received from the labor unions that backed him.</p><p>Bannon conceded to her Tuesday night, as she was leading 2 to 1, both of them told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“I'm like, really overwhelmed because this is fantastic,” she said by phone. “There's…so many teachers that were just rooting for me.</p><p>“Everybody that came up to me said, 'I'm not with the CTU. I don't believe what they're doing'… Ed Bannon was appointed by (Mayor) Brandon Johnson. That was a really big issue up here for me.”</p><p>Voters seeking a change in leadership opted for Luczak, who served on Chicago’s police force for more than 25 years. Her campaign represented a foil to Bannon’s union-backed candidacy.</p><p>She proudly said she’s not a “CTU puppet” and was <a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>supported by contributions</u></a> from the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and The Urban Center, an organization that advocates for centrist leadership and school choice, including private schools. But she has little direct experience in education.</p><p>“I did get donations, and I did have a fundraiser but I didn't have billionaires backing me,” Luczak said. “We are neighborhood people here and the community came out for me.”</p><p>Although the school board elections are nonpartisan, political undercurrents are present in voters’ decisions about which candidate aligns with their values. On the Far Northwest Side, voters have been <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2024/11/06/heres-how-your-neighborhood-voted-in-the-2024-presidential-election-map/" target="_blank" ><u>more receptive to conservative candidates</u></a> than much of Chicago and could be more sympathetic to an “anti-establishment” platform.</p><p>It’s one of the few areas in Chicago that leaned toward President Donald Trump in the 2024 election. And in 2023, many voters here picked former CPS CEO Paul Vallas over Johnson.</p><p>Bannon attributed his defeat to the nature of the district.</p><p>“I think the fundamentals of the district were just too hard to overcome. It was a district that was drawn with a conservative lean to it and that's how the race came out,” he said by phone.</p><p>“I think we ran on the right issues. We need full funding for schools, need to keep public dollars public, need to prevent billionaires from privatizing the education system, but I think those issues weren't as important to voters in that district who, you can see from the last election, that went for Trump and that's how the voters went with this race.”</p><p>Though Bannon was appointed by Johnson, he hasn’t always aligned with him, most notably when he voted last year in favor of <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2025/08/28/cps-board-denies-johnsons-preferred-budget-rejects-pension-payment-and-loan" target="_blank" ><u>the CPS budget plan</u></a> Johnson’s other appointees were trying to block. Bannon’s record earned him endorsements from the Chicago Teachers Union and SEIU Illinois State Council, the other major union representing CPS support staff.</p><p>“I'm happy there's an elected school board. I think that's a victory for Chicago. People have chosen elected officials.”</p><p>This Far Northwest Side district is home to 22 schools that <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=1a" target="_blank" ><u>enroll more white students than Chicago Public Schools as a whole</u></a>, but are more diverse than the voting population. Families here choose their neighborhood public schools at the highest rate in the city — a whopping 75% compared to a citywide average of about 46%.</p><p><i>Contributing:</i><b><i> </i></b><i>Makiya Seminera, Chalkbeat Chicago</i></p>

entries.title: As blue wave sweeps country, Illinois Democrats want to unwind Trump policies ‘as quickly as possible’
entries.summary: <p>Voters across America — and Illinois — sent a loud and clear message to President Donald Trump on Election Night as Democrats flipped seats across the country in a referendum on the president’s aggressive immigration policies, the war in Iran and the economy.</p><p>A strong blue wave means Democrats will provide a check on Trump’s final two years in office and will enact an aggressive legislative agenda to roll back some of the Trump administration’s most unpopular policies. Democrats were able to capitalize on messages about affordability and gas prices, while Republicans sought to paint their Democratic opponents as socialists who would focus on a far-left agenda instead of the economy or a plethora of other issues.</p><p>In Illinois, Democratic members of Congress are hopeful they can begin to pass legislation to unwind Trump policies. To U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, the plan is to “do every damn thing we can to protect them [constituents] as quickly as possible.”</p><p>“I think Democrats need to be able to demonstrate that we're going to do everything in our power to be able to pass the kind of legislation that's going to make their lives better,” Ramirez said on Election Day. </p><p>“Strategically, what I'd like to see is us win the House and Senate, pass everything we possibly can that really brings relief from both chambers," she added. "Leave it to Donald Trump to decide if he wants to be able to take his party in the next election, and then let's make sure that a Democrat wins the White House, so that in fact, when we are there in 2029, we are immediately getting these things signed into law because we've already passed it before.”</p><p>Ramirez, one of the state delegation's most progressive members, said she has her own wish list, including immigration reform, a plan to abolish the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, raising the minimum wage and advancing care through Medicare for All. She also wants to see Democrats take on economic issues like housing and affordability. </p><p>Democratic majorities mean votes will be forced that will require Republicans to take difficult stances and force Trump to either sign or veto legislation. There's also a sense that Republicans will begin realistic conversations about what a post-Trump world will look like — and that Democrats should take advantage of that discussion. </p><p>Democrats are also expected to use the House Oversight Committee to conduct investigations and hearings into the Trump administration, with some in Illinois wanting a focus on White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.</p><p>Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who will become the state's senior senator when Sen. Dick Durbin retires in January, has been a vocal critic of Hegseth, with fiery back-and-forth exchanges going viral during his confirmation hearings and other congressional hearings.</p><p>Duckworth says she voted to impeach Trump three times and would do it again, but she’s more concerned about unwinding damage from cuts stemming from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including saving the state’s nine safety net hospitals and 93 nursing homes from closing. It's on the heavy-handed list she wants to focus on should Democrats win big.</p><p>“And I want to make sure that we restore SNAP benefits, and I want to stop the war in Iran so that we stop sacrificing our brave men and women in uniform to Trump's personal attempts to distract the American people,” Duckworth said. “And yeah, if it's appropriate, then we’ll do the investigations for impeachment. But it's more than just Trump. It’s his Cabinet. It is the people around him, and just their failure to serve the American people as they were charged to do when they were confirmed.”</p><p>As for whether Trump might enact further retribution on blue states after Tuesday's losses, Duckworth said Illinois has seen plenty, but Democrats aren't backing down. </p><p>"The more he tries to bully us, the more we're going to stand up to him," Duckworth said. "Because that's what you do to bullies. You stand up to them and they shrink away."</p>
entries.author: Tina Sfondeles

entries.title: 'Jefe' takes charge: DT Jeffery Simmons embraces role, responsibility as new boss of Bears' defense
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> players couldn’t stop talking about defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons after his dominant debut Monday night in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/02/bears-big-plan-coming-together-beautifully-as-34-17-win-over-seahawks-pushes-them-to-best-start-since-2012" target="_blank" >their 34-17 win over the Seahawks</a>.</p><p>Offense or defense, it didn’t matter. Everyone had something to say.</p><p>They were already happy after he arrived by trade from the Titans last week. They were ecstatic once they saw the impact of one of the NFL’s best defenders blasting into the backfield in a No. 99 Bears jersey.</p><p>Quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> calls him “Jefe,” the Spanish word for “boss.”</p><p>Fellow defensive tackle Grady Jarrett couldn’t wait to get a look at the game film for a better view of how Simmons loosened up the line of scrimmage for him, Montez Sweat, Austin Booker, James Lynch and the other defensive linemen.</p><p>Cornerback Jaylon Johnson answered questions mostly by smiling.</p><p>Simmons embraced all of it, including the responsibility of being the new leader of this defense.</p><p>“You could feel the love,” he said. “Around the building, everyone was excited.</p><p>“But they’re not going to be excited if I’m not out there doing my job. I know what comes with this job. . . . If I’m not doing what I need to do to help this team win, I expect them to hold me to a high standard. It’s a two-way street.”</p><p>Rarely in recent Bears history has a trade looked so good so early. Just days into his time with the team, Simmons seems to be a perfect fit, giving general manager Ryan Poles instant confirmation that it was the right move — not that he needed it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/31/jeffery-simmons-trade-bears-gm-ryan-poles-pursues-legendary-stuff-as-super-bowl-chase-officially-begins" target="_blank" >after feeling confident enough to trade two first-round picks</a> to get his man.</p><p>Simmons and the Bears, it seems, got everything they wanted out of the deal. The team now has a much-needed force at the heart of its defense, and Simmons has jumped from the plummeting Titans into the center of a Super Bowl chase, his excellence no longer wasted in obscurity. Great plays carry a lot more importance here.</p><p>“The last couple of years have been hard, not winning football games, but also, for me, it was like, ‘What can I do to help this team get back to that?’ ” Simmons said. “It sucks that I wasn’t able to do that, but I’m a Chicago Bear now. Things change, and right now for me, to be able to be here, praise God.”</p><p>Simmons led the Bears with six tackles Monday, including a sack in the first quarter and another tackle-for-loss, and was instrumental in Sweat’s stellar game and Lynch’s game-sealing interception. His impact rippled through the defense in subtle ways as well, as the Bears held the Seahawks to one of their worst offensive games of the season.</p><p>That earned him a game ball from coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/16/bears-coach-ben-johnson-is-not-here-merely-to-win-we-want-to-be-feared" target="_blank" >Ben Johnson</a>, who yelled, “Welcome to the Bears, Jeffery Simmons!” while handing the ball to him.</p><p>“I’m so happy to be a [expletive] Chicago Bear,” Simmons answered.</p><p>The Seahawks no doubt would have preferred Poles waiting another week before making the trade. Running backs Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet combined for 49 yards on 16 carries. Quarterback Sam Darnold managed just 188 yards on 17-for-34 passing (his lowest completion percentage of the last two seasons) with two touchdowns and an interception for a 74.1 passer rating.</p><p>The Bears have been calling Simmons as a “multiplier” because they expect he’ll make everyone around him better. It’s an overused term in the NFL, but it certainly applies here, with Simmons’ effect on the defensive line undeniable. The Seahawks doubled him with center Jalen Sundell and guard Grey Zabel on a play in the third quarter play that ended with a sack by Sweat, who ripped past right tackle Abraham Lucas into a wide-open lane. (Sweat’s two other sacks were negated by penalties in the secondary.)</p><p>With the Seahawks desperately trying to rally late, Simmons and Sweat forced Darnold out of the pocket and into the face of Booker, who deflected his pass to Lynch for a pick that squashed the threat.</p><p>Simmons also picked up two, maybe 2½ linemen as Booker, immediately to his right, ran through to block a 33-yard field-goal attempt by Jason Meyers that would have pulled the Seahawks within a touchdown early in the fourth quarter.</p><p>Simmons changed the game for the secondary, too.</p><p>“You know the ball has to come out [on a passing play],” cornerback Johnson said. “It’s a lot easier to cover for two seconds than four, so you can be a little more aggressive.”</p><p>At one point on the sideline, Simmons shouted, “We don’t need to blitz!” because the Bears were getting consistent pressure from the defensive linemen. That’s a game-changer for defensive coordinator Dennis Allen, who had been running the fourth-most blitz-happy unit in the league before Monday.</p><p>“That makes those guys’ job on the back end so much easier,” Simmons said.</p><p>He was conspicuous in every way, including as the only Bear wearing a bright orange sleeved undershirt, which allows his 3-year-old daughter to easily find him on TV. (He wore a red undershirt as a Titan). It also was helpful for Bears fans wanting to zero in on the city’s newest sports star.</p><p>Sleeves or not, you couldn’t miss him. Individually, Simmons played as advertised. Beyond that, he revolutionized the way the Bears played defense.</p><p>For a team adamant that it’s ready to contend for a championship, he sure looks like the missing piece.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: How Bears QB Caleb Williams mastered 'elaborate game plan' vs. Seahawks
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Quarterback Caleb Williams reveled in what felt like the most impactful victory of the Ben Johnson coaching era Monday night by looking into a swath of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> fans at Lumen Field screaming his name.</p><p>He told <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/03/bears-seahawks-34-17-final-score-caleb-williams-i-want-to-make-these-fans-extremely-proud" target="_blank" >ESPN’s Scott Van Pelt</a> that when he was drafted by the Bears, he was told Chicago was always a Bears town, even when Michael Jordan was winning titles with the Bulls. He believed it now, sitting on a studio set more than 2,000 miles away from Halas Hall.</p><p>In the hours that followed, the rest of the United States started acting like that group of navy-clad fans. Williams had 22-1 odds to win the NFL MVP award entering last weekend. He was down to 6-1 by Tuesday morning, behind only the Bills’ Josh Allen, the 49ers’ Brock Purdy and the Bengals’ Joe Burrow.</p><p>Williams — and the Bears — are having a moment.</p><p>What’s remarkable is what it took to get there. Williams didn’t have any jump passes in the Bears’ 34-17 victory against the Seahawks and certainly didn’t have to rally them for a last-second triumph. Rather, Williams willed the offense to success with efficiency.</p><p>He checked into better plays at the line of scrimmage, even with the Seahawks’ faithful at full throat. He made his throws on time. He made few mistakes, becoming only the 14th quarterback all season to throw at least 34 passes in a game, get sacked only once and not throw an interception.</p><p>Given the degree of difficulty — the Seahawks had the NFL’s best defense before Monday — he was remarkable.</p><p>‘‘This was one of the more elaborate game plans in terms of what we were asking him to do,’’ Johnson said. ‘‘That had a lot to do with their scheme. And we needed that out of him to make sure we were getting into a good play that had a chance.’’</p><p>Even when Williams made a mistake, he found a way to fix it. Up by three, the Bears faced third-and-four at the Seahawks’ 39 with about nine minutes left. In the din of a crowd sensing a turning point, Williams took a delay-of-game penalty. The Bears approached the line of scrimmage to run their next play on third-and-nine but were confused. Williams had missed a word in his play-call.</p><p>‘‘The crowd was loud at that point and I missed a word, one word or so,’’ Williams said.</p><p>When officials stopped the game to confer with Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald about whether he wanted to accept the penalty, Williams made sure the Bears lined up properly. He took the snap and threw a sidearm screen to Kalif Raymond, who danced upfield for 39 yards. The Bears scored one play later to seal the victory.</p><p>That didn’t find its way onto Williams’ MVP ledger — it was technically a running play — but it mattered. So did the way he helped trick the Seahawks for the Bears’ first touchdown.</p><p>After Roschon Johnson ran to the Seahawks’ 1 in the first quarter, the Bears went no-huddle, with Williams — and most of his teammates — giving hand signals as though they were going to run the same play again. Instead, Williams faked a handoff to Johnson, rolled right and threw a one-yard touchdown pass to Luther Burden.</p><p>Both those plays take preparation.</p><p>‘‘I want to be my best for Chicago, the organization, my teammates and things like that,’’ Williams said. ‘‘The more that I can do to be able to help this team, I’m going to spend extra time . . . to be able to have all the checks, have all the at-the-line stuff, these funky formations and all these different things to make it seem super-complex for the defense.</p><p>‘‘You put in all the work throughout the week to be able to have this feeling.’’</p><p>On Monday night, the Bears’ fans surrounding Williams could feel it. So could the rest of the country.</p>

entries.title: In upset, LaPamela Williams wins in West Side District 5a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/5a/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 5a</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Austin, Humboldt Park, West Town, Montclare</i></p><p>Realtor LaPamela Williams unseated longtime education activist Aaron “Jitu” Brown to win a spot on the school board representing the West Side’s District 5a.</p><p>Williams, who had the backing of groups supportive of charter schools, received 64% of the vote with nearly 95% of precincts reporting as of early Wednesday morning, according to the Associated Press. She did not respond to a request for comment late Tuesday.</p><p>Williams grew up in Austin and attended Lane Tech College Prep. She’s said she wants to increase financial accountability and cut expenses that don’t benefit students.</p><p>Her triumph over Brown, a veteran community organizer backed by the Chicago Teachers Union, represented an upset. Williams also beat <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/kernetha-jones/" target="_blank" ><u>Kernetha Jones</u></a>, a retired teacher and write-in candidate.</p><p>District 5a stretches from the majority-Black Austin neighborhood to the west, through sections of Garfield Park and Humboldt Park, ending with Ukrainian Village to the east. The wide swath of the West Side encompasses 39 schools serving <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=5a" target="_blank" ><u>mostly Black and Latino students</u></a>. After decades of disinvestment, many schools are <a class="Link" href="https://kidsfirstchicago.org/assets/miscellaneous/2025-Chicagos-Enrollment-Crisis.vF.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>struggling to stabilize enrollment</u></a> and bring students up to grade level.</p><p>More than half of schools in the district last year <a class="Link" href="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SVkXB/1/index.html" target="_blank" ><u>received one of the state’s two lowest academic performance ratings</u></a>, the highest share in the city, indicating many schools are in need of “targeted” or “intensive” support.</p><p>Students who live in District 5a are less likely to attend their neighborhood school than students in most parts of the city, particularly for high school. Less than 7% of high schoolers in this area chose their neighborhood option, according to CPS data. One high school, Frederick Douglass Academy in Austin, had just 27 students last year, and <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2023/11/30/why-does-this-west-side-high-school-only-have-33-students/" target="_blank" ><u>has become a focal point</u></a> in debates over how CPS should address declining enrollment.</p><p>All three candidates live in Austin. Their views diverge when it comes to independently run public charter schools, with Brown and Jones opposing their expansion, while Williams supports opening more if there is community support.</p><p>The Illinois Network of Charter Schools endorsed and financially backed Williams. She was also endorsed by The Urban Center and Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee funded by billionaire Michael Sacks.</p><p>Brown was endorsed and financially supported by the CTU and the CTU-funded group Our Schools Chicago. Jones, the write-in candidate, did not have any major endorsements.</p>

entries.title: Karen Zaccor leads in North Side District 4a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary:
District 4a neighborhoods: Lakeview, Uptown, North Center, Edgewater

Longtime Uptown teacher and incumbent board member Karen Zaccor was leading Tuesday in a three-way race to represent a chunk of the North Side, according to Associated Press election results.

Chicago Teachers Union member Zaccor was narrowly defeating well-funded education consultant Ellen Sherratt and stem cell researcher Angel Alvarez. That’s despite anti-Chicago Teachers Union groups spending more than $300,000 attacking her plus another $300,000 bolstering Sherratt’s campaign.

“I am down by 2,000 votes with 2 precincts yet to report,” Sherratt said late Tuesday night. “It’s not the outcome we hoped for but not inconceivable that a victory is possible either.”

Zaccor was ahead with 44% of the vote to Sherratt’s nearly 39% and Alvarez’s 17%, with 97% of the precincts reporting, according to AP results early Wednesday morning.

The area along the north lakefront is home to 15 schools, less than almost any other school board district. About 57% of students attend their neighborhood elementary schools — a little higher than the 46% citywide average — but that share is much lower for high school. The district serves a diverse student body; about 35% are Hispanic, 27% are white, almost 24% are Black and nearly 8% are Asian, according to data compiled by Chalkbeat.

Zaccor has voted consistently with a majority bloc of board members also appointed by Mayor Brandon Johnson or elected with backing from the Chicago Teachers Union, Johnson’s former employer and close ally. Her priorities also echo those of the union, which endorsed Zaccor. They include pushing for a billionaires tax or other progressive state revenue to boost school funding.

Her opponents Sherratt and Alvarez argued that the district must do more to address mounting deficits than lobby the state.

Sherratt drew endorsements from the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents support staff and has split politically with the teachers union in recent years, and other groups that oppose the CTU. Those include the Common Ground Collective, an anti-CTU political action committee.

Common Ground and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools have spent more than $600,000 on this race, attacking Zaccor as they bolstered Sherratt. And Sherratt has raised more than $260,000 individually — the most of all candidates, as of Monday. Alvarez had no outside PAC support.

Sherratt had said she would push for setting ambitious student achievement goals.

Alvarez, who leads a family advisory board for the district, said he would champion more responsive special education and protect families from higher property taxes.

Contributing: Mila Koumpilova of Chalkbeat Chicago
